name: Salt-misted firebreak
subtitle: a strip of brush kept damp by salt

effects.effect: some substances pull water out of the air

effect: some substances pull water out of the air
how: Wildfires race through grass and brush dried to a crisp, and firebreaks often aren't wide enough to stop the flames. Spraying a strip of vegetation with a salt such as calcium chloride, which pulls water from the air (hygroscopy), keeps that strip damp for weeks, so flames reaching it slow down and crews can hold them there.
obstacle: In the driest fire weather the air falls below the humidity at which even calcium chloride can draw in water, and the salt harms soil and streams.
why: Wildfires are getting worse; a cheap way to keep firebreaks damp could save towns.
real: Perimeter-style long-term retardant patents claim magnesium/calcium chloride solutions pull moisture into fuels to retard fire; no independent field trials of a hygroscopic-salt firebreak found.
